episode.title: Cariboo Signals - Cariboo Local Affairs
episode.description:
Riley and Casey explore technology and society in rural communities. Today's focus: Cariboo Local Affairs.

THIS WEEK WE'RE ASKING: How much should neighbours know about each other?

NEWS ROUNDUP: We break down City of Williams Lake seeks public feedback to guide future of parks and trails and Made in the Cariboo Christmas Market celebrates locally made products, plus 10 more stories, and explore what these developments mean for communities like ours.

RURAL CONNECTIONS: When a small town cannot fund its own infrastructure, does taking the problem to a regional association give its council real control, or do decisions stay with whoever holds the grants? Topics include: Asset management and grant dependence in small-town infrastructure planning, Regional association resolutions and who answers them, Living wage pressures and property tax versus user fee burdens on households, Local ownership and procurement rules, using the TEN and Dandzen example, Public records of refused requests, deferred projects, and provincial tax cuts and transfers.

Hosts: Riley (Tech optimist with an engineering background) and Casey (Community-first skeptic of tech promises).

COMMUNITY SPOTLIGHT: CMHA Cariboo Chilcotin

discussion.central_question: When a small town cannot fund its own infrastructure, does taking the problem to a regional association give its council real control, or do decisions stay with whoever holds the grants?
discussion.riley_position: Riley argues that asset management and a regional resolution give small councils real leverage and a choice over their own projects, and that councils should write procurement rules and publish the record of refused requests so residents can see where decisions are made.
riley_key_evidence: The 2026 Living Wage Report found no B.C. community where the $18.25 minimum wage covers a living wage, with Whistler at $30.50 and Grand Forks at $22.15.
Dandzen Development, the economic development arm of the Tŝilhqot'in National Government, founded TEN in 2017 and holds 51 per cent of it.
Barriere Mayor Rob Kerslake brought a resolution to the Southern Interior Local Government Association convention asking for a broader conversation on municipal infrastructure funding.
discussion.casey_position: Casey argues that grant-dependent infrastructure plans are precarious, that resolutions and rules are only as strong as the budgets behind them, and that the real test is whether plans show lines for grants that never arrive and publish deferred projects alongside wanted ones.
casey_key_evidence: Kerslake calls grant programs precarious, and a five-year plan cannot rest on something a budget cycle can cut.
Williams Lake council approved $150,000 in the 2025 Capital Budget to update its parks plan, yet nothing in the coverage names a capital line to fund it.
Cranbrook has over $40 million in project costs over ten years, including $8.3 million for Western Financial Place alone, and deferred projects are rarely voted on or published.
discussion.resolution: The two agreed that the decision record should be kept public at the council table, with copies held by the regional association and the province, and that councils should publish both wanted and deferred project lists with the same dates. They did not settle whether the resolution passed or whether the province will answer it.

research.block:
PRE-RESEARCHED INSIGHTS FOR THE DEEP DIVE
These analytical threads were identified before generation. Use the findings to ground Riley's and Casey's arguments with real evidence — develop them as substantive exchanges, not a citation list. Cite naturally.

RESEARCH QUESTION: Did the Quesnel defamation ruling turn on the merits of the residential school book claims, or on a procedural anti-SLAPP-style protection for public participation?
Findings: Multiple outlets (The Northern View, The Free Press, Williams Lake Tribune and others carrying the same wire story) report that Justice Tindale ruled Coun. Laurey-Anne Roodenburg's statements about Pat Morton's distribution of a book questioning the findings surrounding residential schools were protected under the Protection of Public Participation Act (B.C.'s anti-SLAPP law). The ruling was published Nov. 10 and the suit is dismissed. The reported basis is the statute's public-participation protection, not a finding on whether the book's claims about residential schools are accurate. The dispute arose from comments at a 2024 council meeting.
Suggested angle: This is a useful test of where the line sits between council debate and reputational harm. Riley can argue the ruling shows the system working: an elected official's words in a public meeting get strong protection, and a quick dismissal keeps small-town councils from being chilled by lawsuits. Casey can counter that the court never judged whether the book's claims were true, so the case leaves the community's trust in residential school history unresolved, and a rural council is a place where a weak defamation suit can still be costly and divisive. Ask both whether the anti-SLAPP tool protects a councillor only when the speech is about public matters, and whether that protection holds when the topic touches Indigenous survivors' accounts.

RESEARCH QUESTION: How large is the minimum wage versus living wage gap in B.C. communities in the 2026 report, and what does it mean for Cariboo residents?
Findings: Living Wage BC and BC Policy Solutions released the 2026 Living Wage Report on Nov. 19, 2026 (reported by My Cariboo Now). The minimum wage is $18.25/hour (raised June 1, 2026). The report says there is no community in B.C. where that minimum covers basic costs. Whistler has the highest living wage at $30.50, which is $12.25 above minimum wage; Grand Forks is the lowest at $22.15; Metro Vancouver is $28.55; Golden is the only community where the figure was unchanged, at $27.80. The gap widened in almost every tracked community. The report attributes cost pressure to shelter, food, child care, and fuel, with trade policy and the conflict in Iran cited for fuel and clothing costs. Living Wage BC has called for a $20 minimum wage. Co-author Navdeep Chhina said the incoming B.C. Conservatives' affordability pledges could help through income tax cuts, but cuts to health, education, or transportation could hurt, and rental, transportation, and food access matter more. The report also credits existing measures such as the Canadian Dental Care Plan and BC Rental Assistance Program increases.
Suggested angle: Riley can argue that the numbers show a clear policy lever: a $20 floor or targeted affordability measures could close part of the gap, and that federal and provincial benefits are already reducing pressure. Casey can push back that the living wage is a modeled figure based on average costs in major communities, not a measured local budget, and that a higher minimum wage can cost jobs in small Cariboo employers with thin margins and seasonal work, so the gap may be a symptom of housing and transport costs rather than wage policy alone. Both should consider whether Grand Forks' lower figure compared with Whistler says something about how rural costs translate into wage needs.

RESEARCH QUESTION: What is the context behind B.C. mayors' push for municipal infrastructure funding reform, led by Barriere Mayor Rob Kerslake?
Findings: Reporting from Nov. 20, 2026 (carried across Vista/Black Press titles, including the Williams Lake Tribune) says Barriere Mayor Rob Kerslake is seeking a broader conversation about how municipal infrastructure is funded. He argues the infrastructure funding gap "is not a new topic," that it has been around "for a while," and that grant programs are precarious. Barriere faces significant critical infrastructure costs in the coming years. The full article was not retrieved, so specific dollar figures and the names of other mayors involved could not be verified here.
Suggested angle: Riley can frame this as a practical fix: predictable, formula-based transfers in place of one-off grants would let small towns like Barriere plan capital upgrades. Casey can ask whether the problem is the funding mechanism or the fact that small communities take on costs they cannot sustain. Each should ask who pays for the gap, whether through senior-government transfers, property tax, or user fees, and whether a rural tax base can ever cover ageing water and road systems without outside money.

roundup.opening_frame: A community-minded Cariboo news day, with local events and recognition alongside a new provincial government taking shape and a few stories about how places plan and prepare.

stories.point: The City of Williams Lake has launched public engagement to update its 2011 Parks and Trails Plan, funded with $150,000 approved in the 2025 Capital Budget.

More than 700 people visited 28 vendors at the Made in the Cariboo Christmas Market at the Williams Lake Tourism Discovery Centre on Nov. 14, including first-time vendor Chad Marchand with his hardwood cutting boards.
Ever After Attire's Borrowed Magic pop-up on Saturday, Nov. 21, from noon to 3 p.m. at the Central Cariboo Arts and Culture Centre lets Williams Lake graduates borrow an outfit for free.
The 100 Mile House Santa Claus Parade has 53 floats entered and runs Friday, Nov. 27 at 5:30 p.m. on Birch Avenue, with a Griswold Family Christmas theme.
Williams Lake's Tyson Delay placed second in the 105 kg class at the Canadian Strongman Championships in Quebec.

Lorne Doerkson was sworn in as B.C.'s premier on Nov. 20 after the Conservatives won 64 of 93 seats. There will be no fall legislative session, a tax cut is planned as soon as Jan. 1, SOGI 123 is to be ended immediately, and a finance review is coming, while repealing DRIPA waits until spring.
A black bear that found food in an open garage in Revelstoke injured a 16-year-old on Nov. 14 and was destroyed.
The 100 Mile House RCMP have identified a driver in a Nov. 11 Highway 97 hit-and-run near Spring Lake Road, who left after asking that police not be called.
Bob Zimmerman, the former longtime president of Quesnel Search and Rescue, received the national Emergency Management Exemplary Service Award after 37 years of service.
Williams Lake residents have until Sunday, Nov. 22 to drop off Operation Christmas Child shoeboxes at Evangelical Free Church, after the city shipped 451 boxes in 2025.
Interim B.C. NDP Leader Jennifer Whiteside is urging the incoming government to oppose Quebecor's $31-billion bid for Telus, warning of less competition and higher prices.
stories.bridge_to_next: Telecommunications: a telecom outage is what grounded U.S. flights in the next story.

stories.point: A telecommunications outage led the FAA to ground all U.S. planes on Nov. 13, causing about 3,600 cancellations.
Nazko First Nation members voted unanimously to add the Three Nations Store and Lodge property to the Nation's reserve land base, pending federal review.
Canadian Armed Forces search and rescue crews are training with flares in the Chilcotin Military Training Area, about 50 km southwest of Williams Lake, from Nov. 16 to 20.
A facility assessment shows Cranbrook faces over $40 million in project costs at city facilities over the next decade, with Western Financial Place the largest at $8.3 million.

The RCMP suspended the official search for Ma'amtagila Nation member James Dakota Smith, missing since Nov. 6 near Sayward, because of storm conditions, while his family and community keep searching and seek government support.

roundup.handoff: Williams Lake's parks plan and Cranbrook's $40 million facility list both show towns planning decades of upkeep, which leads into how a small town like Barriere pays for what it has to maintain.

deep_dive.central_question: When a town of about 1,000 ratepayers faces multi-million dollar infrastructure bills it cannot cover from its own tax base, does taking the problem to a regional local government association give that town's council real control over its future, or does it leave the real decisions with whoever controls the grants?
deep_dive.riley_holds: Riley thinks a council that does its asset management honestly and brings a resolution to a body like SILGA is doing the right thing, and that community-owned capacity like TEN shows small places can build their own options.
deep_dive.casey_holds: Casey thinks a resolution and an asset plan do not change who holds the money, and that a town reliant on precarious grants is deciding in name only unless the system itself changes.

beats.claim: Barriere's asset management work has shown the town a funding problem that its own ratepayers cannot solve, so the council's choices are narrowed before it votes.
beats.evidence: Mayor Rob Kerslake says that as Barriere digs deeper into asset management it finds multi-million dollar projects to fund, which for a town of 1,000 ratepayers is near impossible (Williams Lake Tribune).
beats.leads_to_next: If the problem is the system and not one council, the question becomes where a small council can press for change, which is the route Kerslake took.

beats.claim: Taking a resolution to SILGA is a real use of civic voice, because it turns one town's problem into something other local governments can vote on.
beats.evidence: Kerslake brought a resolution to the Southern Interior Local Government Association convention aimed at reforming how municipal infrastructure is funded and at the precarity of relying on grants (Williams Lake Tribune).
beats.pushback: Casey: the article describes a resolution and a call to start a conversation, not a commitment from the province. The funding gap is described as an old topic, so a resolution is a request for others to decide, not a decision.
beats.leads_to_next: If the request leaves the decision with others, we need to know who bears the cost while a town waits, which the living wage report shows from the household side.

beats.claim: Ratepayers cannot simply fill the gap, because household costs are already outrunning wages in nearly every tracked community, so council decisions about taxes sit against that squeeze.
beats.evidence: The Living Wage report says the gap between minimum wage and living wage grew in almost every tracked community, and that no community's living wage could be met by the $18.25 minimum wage; the highest living wage is Whistler at $30.50 and the lowest Grand Forks at $22.15 (My Cariboo Now).
beats.pushback: Riley: the report covers household costs, not municipal tax capacity, so it shows the pressure on residents but cannot say Barriere's ratepayers could not carry any of the bill; that is for the town's own asset plan to show.
beats.leads_to_next: If household budgets limit what a town can ask of ratepayers, the next test is whether any local body has built its own capacity so its decisions do not depend on outside grants.

beats.claim: Locally owned capacity can change who decides, as the Tŝilhqot'in National Government's construction company shows, but it works for a Nation with its own governing structure and may not transfer to a village council.
beats.evidence: Dandzen Development LP, the economic arm of the Tŝilhqot'in National Government, founded TEN in 2017 and holds 51 per cent; TEN was founded to make roads safer in Tŝilhqot'in territory and diversify the local economy amid a forestry downturn, and has partnered with Kamloops-based Dawson Civil to expand across B.C. (Williams Lake Tribune).
beats.pushback: Casey: TEN's growth now relies on a partnership with an outside firm and work across B.C., so local ownership has meant going beyond the home territory for work, which a town of 1,000 ratepayers cannot do.
beats.leads_to_next: If ownership and outside partnership both matter, what a town can reasonably demand is that the way its infrastructure gets funded is visible in its own public record, which sets up the landing.

set_aside: Defamation suit dismissed over residential school book controversy in Quesnel council: a council-and-resident dispute already argued in earlier debates and not about how towns fund and decide infrastructure.
Addictions Awareness Week 24-foot community mural in Williams Lake: aired in Thursday's roundup, and it concerns a community art project rather than a civic funding decision.
deep_dive.cariboo_beat: The TEN beat brings it home to the Tŝilhqot'in National Government and Dandzen Development LP in the Cariboo-Chilcotin, which built its own construction company with a 51 per cent stake and now partners with an outside firm.
deep_dive.landing: Held open: when a small town's infrastructure depends on grants decided elsewhere, should the record of what it asked for and was refused sit with the town council, the regional association that carries its resolution, or the province, so residents can see where the decision was actually made?
